title: Medical Chronology Builder
description: Hash-group then sort — group medical records by date into a Map, then emit dates in sorted order with same-date events kept in input order.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Building a medical chronology is something legal-tech engineers see weekly — every personal-injury case needs one — and the interviewer probes ordering, duplicate handling, and date robustness. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Spec-heavy problem — clarifying questions are the signal.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm building `buildChronology(records)` where each record is `{date, provider, note}`. Output is one line per date, chronological, with same-date events collapsed onto that one line separated by `'; '`. Before I code, the questions that actually decide the implementation:"

• What format are dates in? If they're ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`), I can sort them as plain strings — no Date parsing. If they're `MM/DD/YYYY` or mixed, I need to parse first.
• Within a date, what order — input order, alphabetical by provider, or some other stable rule? Input order is the usual answer because it preserves the source's intent.
• Duplicates — two records with the same date, provider, AND note. Collapse to one line item or keep both? Usually keep both verbatim; dedup is a separate pass.
• Timezone — do I care? For medical records `YYYY-MM-DD` is date-only, no TZ; for incident times that span midnight, it matters.
• What about records with no date — drop, group under `'unknown'`, or throw? Defensively, I'd group under `'unknown'` and put it at the end, never throw.
• Scale — am I building one chronology (1000 records) or a million? Determines whether I need streaming.
sections.why: The ISO-vs-non-ISO date question is the load-bearing one. If dates are ISO, the implementation is dramatically simpler — `String.prototype.sort()` is chronological. If not, you're parsing every date into a `Date` object and writing a comparator. Most candidates skip this clarification and write the harder version unnecessarily. The within-date ordering question is the second-most-important: input order means `.push` into the bucket; alphabetical means sort the bucket. The legal-tech context strongly suggests input-order — the source document already has the intent.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious version before discarding it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: sort the full records array by date, then iterate and emit each record on its own line. That gives me chronological output but doesn't COLLAPSE same-date events — `2024-02-01 ER admitted` and `2024-02-01 Radiology CT` would be two lines instead of one combined.

To collapse, I'd need a 'previous date' tracker in the loop: emit a new line if `r.date !== prevDate`, otherwise append to the current buffer. That works but it mixes two concerns — sorting and grouping — and gets brittle when records on the same date arrive out of order in the input.

"Cleaner: separate the two phases. First, GROUP by date into a Map. Second, EMIT sorted by date key. Two passes, but each one is doing one thing. Now within-date ordering is just whatever order I pushed (input order), and chronological output is just sorting the date keys."
sections.why: The brute-force-then-refactor walk is the right way to land on group-then-sort — saying 'sort then iterate' first and then noticing 'oh, that gets brittle when same-date records aren't adjacent in the input' makes the Map feel like a derivation, not a magic trick. Splitting the two concerns (group + sort) is a senior-tier code-design move that an interviewer notices.

sections.title: 3. Spot the shape — hash-group then sort
sections.prompt: What's the structural property that picks Map-keyed-state?
sections.why: Naming the shape — hash-group-then-sort — is what distinguishes this from 'I used a Map'. The 'ISO is lex-chronological' observation is the load-bearing insight that lets you skip Date parsing; without naming it, you'd reach for `new Date(a) - new Date(b)` in the sort comparator and ship slower, error-prone code. The Map-vs-Object choice is the JS-specific signal an interviewer notices — Object keys are always strings and don't preserve numeric insertion order; Map sidesteps both.

sections.title: 4. Trace through a tiny example
sections.prompt: Walk a 3-record input through the two phases.
sections.intro: "Let me run the L3 input — three records, deliberately out of date order, with two sharing 2024-02-01."

examples.input: records=[{date:'2024-02-01', provider:'ER', note:'Admitted'}, {date:'2024-01-15', provider:'PCP', note:'Initial visit'}, {date:'2024-02-01', provider:'Radiology', note:'CT scan'}]
examples.output: ["2024-01-15 — PCP: Initial visit", "2024-02-01 — ER: Admitted; Radiology: CT scan"]
examples.note: Out-of-order input with two same-date records — proves the group-then-sort approach is order-independent in the input.
Single record — confirms the happy path doesn't depend on having duplicates.
examples.trace:
Phase 1: byDate={'2024-03-10':['PT: session 1']}
Phase 2: keys=['2024-03-10'], sorted same, emit one line.

examples.note: Empty input — both phases no-op cleanly, return [].
examples.trace:
Phase 1: loop doesn't fire, byDate stays empty Map.
Phase 2: [...byDate.keys()] = [], .sort() = [], .map(...) = [] → return [].

sections.why: The first trace is the one to narrate out loud — same-date records arriving non-adjacent in the input is the most common gotcha. A naive `if (r.date === prevDate) appendToCurrentLine else newLine` would emit THREE lines instead of two on this input, because the ER record and Radiology record aren't adjacent. The group-into-Map first ELIMINATES that ordering dependency. The empty-input case isn't padding — it's confirming the canonical's two phases each no-op gracefully, which is what the interviewer asks about under 'edge cases'.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & failure modes
sections.prompt: Medical records are dirty — what real-world inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging — most come from real medical data uglies:"

• Empty input — return `[]`. The two phases both no-op; the canonical handles it without a special case. ✓
• Single record — one bucket, one output line. ✓
• All records on one date — one bucket of N events, one output line with N events joined. The grouping shape gets stress-tested but doesn't change.
• Same date, same provider, same note (true duplicate) — current code keeps both, which is probably what you want (the medical record was filed twice). If dedup is wanted, that's a pre-pass — call it out as a separate concern.
• Missing/null date — `r.date` is undefined. The Map key becomes `undefined`, which `.sort()` puts at the end of the string sort. Defensively, I'd group under `'unknown'` and append after the dated section. Worth confirming with the interviewer.
• Non-ISO date format — `'01/15/2024'`. Lex sort would put `'01/15/2024'` before `'02/01/2024'` correctly but `'12/31/2023'` AFTER `'01/15/2024'` because `'1'` > `'0'`. Catches you blind. Pre-normalize to ISO or comparator-based sort.
• Mixed timezones — `'2024-01-15T08:00:00-05:00'` vs `'2024-01-15T13:00:00Z'`. As date-only strings, they sort by the prefix only, but if you start using `new Date()` you'd see them at different times. For chronology that says 'on this date' the date prefix is enough; for time-of-day matters (incident timing) you'd switch to full timestamps.
• PII in note text — SSNs, DOBs, address strings. The chronology builder doesn't redact; that's a downstream pass. Worth flagging that you'd run the output through a redactor before sharing.
• Provider name containing `';'` — would break the `.split('; ')` of consumers who try to undo the join. Edge case; usually handled by escaping or by using a structured output format (array of arrays).
sections.why: The non-ISO date trap is the one that catches careless candidates — `MM/DD/YYYY` looks sortable but isn't, and the bug only shows up when months cross a 10-boundary. Naming this unprompted shows you know WHY ISO-lex works (fixed-width, big-endian) and what breaks it. The PII separation-of-concerns call-out is the legal-tech-aware signal — you're not pretending one function does everything. The provider-with-semicolon edge is the test-of-test thinking: who consumes this output? If it's a downstream `.split('; ')`, you're vulnerable.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & memory
sections.prompt: Defend the bounds with the actual amortization.
sections.say:
"Time is O(n + k log k) where n = number of records, k = number of distinct dates. Phase 1 (group) is O(n) — each record is one Map operation and one push, both amortized O(1). Phase 2 (sort) is O(k log k) — sorting the distinct date keys, where k ≤ n. The emit pass is O(n) because every record gets joined into exactly one bucket.

Space is O(n) — the Map holds one entry per record across all its buckets. Plus the output array which is O(k) lines, each containing a slice of the n events.

"For extensions: if dates are sortable on read (you control the input), you could skip the explicit sort and just iterate records once, maintaining a 'last-seen date' running max. But that only works if input is monotonically increasing — fragile. The group-then-sort approach is the robust default and the cost is negligible at typical chronology sizes (≤10K records per case).

"At true scale — millions of records across thousands of cases — you'd shift this to a database query: `SELECT date, GROUP_CONCAT(provider || ': ' || note ORDER BY id SEPARATOR '; ') FROM records GROUP BY date ORDER BY date`. The shape's identical; you're just delegating the group + sort to the storage layer that's optimized for it."
sections.why: The k log k vs n distinction matters — if a candidate says 'O(n)' without acknowledging the sort, the interviewer probes. The 'monotonically-increasing-input' extension is the prove-you-thought-about-it move: you considered the streaming optimization and discarded it as fragile. Naming the SQL equivalent unprompted is the senior-tier signal — you see this pattern as language-agnostic group-by, not as a JS-specific Map trick.

sections.title: 7. Robustness & tests
sections.prompt: Legal docs care about correctness — how would you add tests?
sections.say:
"Tests I'd write, in order:"

• Happy path — multiple dates with multiple records per date, output exactly chronological.
• Out-of-order input — same records in random order produces same output (the group-then-sort guarantee).
• Single date — N records on one day collapse to one line with N events joined by `'; '`.
• Empty input → `[]`.
• Within-date ordering — two records on same date in input order A then B emit `A; B`, not `B; A`.
• Missing date — `{provider, note}` with no `date`. Confirm the contract with interviewer; if 'unknown' group, assert it appears at the end.
• Non-ISO date — if you support `MM/DD/YYYY`, test that 12/31/2023 sorts BEFORE 01/15/2024 (the lex-trap).
• True duplicate records — both rendered, no silent dedup.
• Property test — generate random shuffles of a known-chronology input, assert output is invariant under shuffling. Strong test for the order-independence claim.

"In a real legal-tech codebase I'd also add a contract test: feed the output of `buildChronology` back into a parser that reconstructs `{date, provider, note}` records, assert round-trip identity. Catches join-character collisions (provider containing `';'`) before they hit production. The shape is symmetrical — group-then-sort is the inverse of split-then-merge."
sections.why: Property-based testing for 'order independence' is the senior touch — most candidates write a few example tests; suggesting a property test for the structural claim of the algorithm shows you're thinking about the SHAPE of the correctness, not just specific inputs. The round-trip contract test is the legal-tech-aware move: in production you care that no information was silently lost or corrupted, and a parse-then-format round-trip is the cheapest way to catch it.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the two-phase chronology builder: Phase 1 groups records into a Map by date (note how out-of-order input doesn't matter), Phase 2 sorts the date keys (ISO lex = chronological) and emits one line per date. State panel shows the growing `byDate` Map, then the sorted keys, then the emitted `out` array.

examples.label: 3 records, out of order, 2 share a date
examples.expected: ["2024-01-15 — PCP: Initial visit","2024-02-01 — ER: Admitted; Radiology: CT scan"]

trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter — ${records.length} records`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()] } };
yield { line: 2, label: `Phase 1: GROUP into Map keyed by date`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()] } };
yield { line: 3, label: `record#${k}: date=${r.date}, provider=${r.provider}, note=${JSON.stringify(r.note)}`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], r, k } };
yield { line: 4, label: `new date — lazy init byDate.set(${JSON.stringify(r.date)}, [])`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], r, k } };
yield { line: 4, label: `date already has bucket — skip init`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], r, k } };
yield { line: 5, label: `push ${JSON.stringify(entry)} into bucket for ${r.date}`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], r, k } };
yield { line: 6, label: `Phase 1 done — ${byDate.size} distinct date(s) grouped`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()] } };
yield { line: 7, label: `Phase 2: SORT keys — insertion order = ${JSON.stringify(insertionKeys)}`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], insertionKeys } };
yield { line: 8, label: `keys.sort() = ${JSON.stringify(sortedKeys)} (ISO lex = chronological)`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], insertionKeys, sortedKeys } };
yield { line: 9, label: `emit ${JSON.stringify(line)}`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], sortedKeys, out: [...out] } };
yield { line: 10, label: `return out — ${out.length} chronology line(s)`, state: { records, byDate: [...byDate.entries()], out: [...out], returns: JSON.stringify(out) } };

notes: ISO 8601 dates (YYYY-MM-DD) are lexicographically sortable: a plain string `.sort()` gives chronological order, so you never need to parse them into Date objects here.
`if (!byDate.has(r.date)) byDate.set(r.date, [])` lazily initializes the bucket; without it the first `.get(...).push` on a new date would throw on `undefined`.
Same-date records collapse in INPUT order because `.push` appends — sorting only reorders the date keys, never the events within a date.
Time O(n + k log k), Space O(n) — n = number of records (Phase 1 group); k = distinct dates (Phase 2 sort, k ≤ n).

questions.q: Why are the records grouped into a `Map` keyed by date before emitting?
options: Sorting `records` directly would shuffle same-date entries because `.sort()` isn't stable on equal keys
So that all events sharing a date land in one bucket, ready to collapse into a single output line
An Object keyed by date would coerce ISO dates to milliseconds, breaking the prefix sort
Map iteration runs in parallel via web workers, which speeds up the emit phase
questions.explain: The group-then-emit shape collects same-date events into one bucket so each date produces exactly one collapsed line.

questions.q: Why does `[...byDate.keys()].sort()` produce chronological order without parsing dates?
options: `Map.prototype.keys()` returns keys in sorted order; the explicit `.sort()` is a defensive no-op
ISO 8601 dates (YYYY-MM-DD) sort the same lexicographically as chronologically
The hyphen character has a numeric collation weight that aligns string and date order
`.sort()` falls back to `Date.parse` when every element passes a date-shape heuristic
questions.explain: Fixed-width YYYY-MM-DD strings compare character-by-character in the same order as the calendar, so a plain string sort is chronological.

questions.q: Two records share the date 2024-02-01. What determines their order on the output line?
options: The order they appeared in the input (the `.push` order)
Whichever record's `.join('; ')` call fired first during the emit pass
The order matching the buckets' sort by event count, ascending
questions.explain: Sorting only reorders the date keys. Within a date, `.push` keeps events in the order they were read from the input.

questions.q: What is the purpose of `if (!byDate.has(r.date)) byDate.set(r.date, [])`?
options: It overwrites any existing bucket so repeated dates don't accumulate stale events from a prior call
It lazily creates an empty array bucket the first time a date is seen, so the later `.get().push` won't throw
It registers the date with the Map's internal sort index so the later `[...keys()].sort()` is O(1)
It prevents `byDate.get` from returning the Map's default value of `null` instead of `undefined`
questions.explain: Without initializing the bucket, `byDate.get(r.date)` would be `undefined` on a first-seen date and `.push` would throw.

exercises.prompt: Lazily initialize a Map bucket and push into it, then read it back. Fill the blanks so the output is the joined notes.
ISO date strings sort chronologically as plain strings. Fill the blanks so the dates print earliest-first.

blanks.hint: default lexicographic sort works for ISO dates

L3.prompt: Turn a list of medical records (`{date, provider, note}`) into a chronological timeline. Sort by date; records on the same date collapse into one line, joined by `; `.
L3.expectedOutput:
2024-01-15 — PCP: Initial visit
2024-02-01 — ER: Admitted; Radiology: CT scan
hints: Group first: a Map keyed by `r.date`, each value an array of `provider: note` strings.
Lazily create the bucket with `if (!byDate.has(r.date)) byDate.set(r.date, [])` before pushing.
Emit by sorting the keys (ISO dates sort chronologically as strings) and joining each bucket with `'; '`.
